Fertilised eggs of white seabass, Atractoscion nobilis, measure approximately 0.8 cm in diameter, and the newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges at a remarkably small size. The wet weight at birth is 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], reflecting the tiny, pelagic egg characteristic of this sciaenid. Following the period of yolk absorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, larvae enter a planktonic phase where rapid growth is driven by the productive waters of the eastern Pacific. As the larvae develop, they undergo a pronounced morphological transformation into postflexion stages before settling into coastal habitats as juveniles. Under the thermal conditions of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], a temperature typical of the broodstock holding tanks used in aquaculture facilities, the daily reproductive rate can be estimated. Gravid females, having reached an appropriate condition, may release multiple batches of eggs over a protracted spawning season. The annual fecundity is substantial, reflecting the species' high reproductive potential. Maximum adult body size is notable for the genus, with individuals reaching a total length of 166 cm [Li = 166 cm], a size that places them among the larger members of the croaker family.

Sexual maturation in white seabass is closely tied to body size rather than strictly to age. Individuals typically attain puberty at a total length of 61 cm [Lp = 61 cm], a developmental milestone that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the capacity for reproductive contribution to the population. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is roughly 2 kilograms [Wwp = roughly 2 kilograms], a mass that must be achieved through sustained foraging success during the juvenile and sub-adult phases. Growth to this size often occurs over several growing seasons, and the length-based onset of maturity serves as a critical life history parameter for stock assessment models. The fecundity data at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] indicate that each female can produce approximately 21,918 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 21,918 eggs per day] when reproductive activity is sustained over the spawning window. This high daily output is a common life-history strategy among iteroparous, broadcast-spawning marine fishes that offset high larval mortality with massive gamete release. The ultimate wet weight recorded for white seabass is 41 kilograms [Wwi = 41 kilograms], a substantial body mass that is attained only by the oldest and largest individuals in the population. Achieving this size requires decades of continuous growth and is limited by both food availability and the energetic demands of reproduction. In contrast, the enormous fecundity at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] demonstrates the species' capacity for population resilience. At a sustained production rate of 21,918 eggs daily [Ri = 21,918 eggs daily], the annual reproductive output of a single large female is staggering, though the vast majority of these pelagic eggs will never survive to the juvenile stage. The larval period is a critical bottleneck; after hatching at 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], the tiny larvae are vulnerable to starvation and predation until they reach the postflexion stage and become more capable foragers. Population dynamics are thus heavily influenced by interannual variation in oceanographic conditions that affect larval survival and, consequently, recruitment to the adult population.

Comparative life-history analyses place the white seabass within a slow-to-moderate pace-of-life continuum relative to other large sciaenids. The total length at puberty of 61 cm [Lp = 61 cm] represents a considerable delay in reproductive onset when scaled against body size, a pattern that aligns with energy allocation toward sustained somatic growth before first reproduction. The wet weight of 2 kilograms [Wwp = 2 kilograms] at puberty further underscores the substantial resource investment required to initiate reproductive capability. The daily egg production of 21,918 eggs per day [Ri = 21,918 eggs per day] carried out at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] is comparable to the fecundity reported for the closely related weakfish, though the white seabass attains a larger maximum size of 166 cm [Li = 166 cm]. A typical female can therefore produce more eggs per spawning season simply by virtue of her larger body cavity and the extended spawning period, which can last several months. This bet-hedging strategy, combining delayed maturity with high fecundity, is well suited to an environment where recruitment success is highly variable from year to year.

Longevity data from mark-recapture studies and otolith analysis confirm that the maximum lifespan of white seabass is approximately 28 years [am = approximately 28 years], a duration that under the thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] allows for multiple reproductive seasons across an individual's lifetime. The ultimate total length of 166 cm [Li = 166 cm] combined with an asymptotic body mass of 41 kilograms [Wwi = 41 kilograms] indicates that growth slows markedly after sexual maturity is reached, a pattern common among long-lived marine fishes. The wet weight of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] at birth stands in stark contrast to the adult mass, representing a several-million-fold increase over the lifespan. This extreme size disparity between the planktonic larva and the demersal adult highlights the profound ecological transition the species undergoes. Conservation and management efforts must account for these life-history traits: the delayed puberty at 61 cm [Lp = 61 cm] and the slow attainment of ultimate size mean that heavy fishing pressure can quickly deplete the reproductive population, as older, larger individuals are disproportionately removed from the spawning stock before they have contributed maximally to recruitment.
